v0.2.0 was about what you look at. This one is about what you can name, and there is less to learn than there was: three pairs of things collapsed into one each.

**One log**

fufu kept two timelines. `refs/fufu/snap/<branch>` held snapshots and `refs/fufu/journal` held operations — two id schemes, two prefix resolvers, two trim mechanisms, two trash refs. Measured on this repository at the time: 1584 snapshots against 64 journal entries, only a handful of which referenced a snapshot at all. So almost everything fufu had captured belonged to no operation, and answered to a different address than the one you would ask with.

They are one log now, at `refs/fufu/ops`. Every capture is an operation and a snapshot is what an operation carries, so there is one timeline, one id space, and one family of verbs that reads it. The per-branch ref survives only as a pointer into that log, moved in the same transaction as the tip.

`ff op` is that family: `log` lists every operation newest first, `show` and `diff` read them, `restore` rewinds the whole repository to one, and `revert` inverts a single one while later work stands. Deleting operations is `ff trim`'s job and nobody else's. Operation ids stay in the letters k–z and never in hex, which is what keeps hex meaning "commit" everywhere in fufu without exception, and git's own first-parent suffixes work on them — `@^` is the operation before, `@~3` three back — because an operation's first parent *is* the operation before it.

`ff undo` steps by runs. A capture is a machine's granularity and a person's undo is not, so undo steps over the longest stretch of adjacent captures sharing a session; a verb's operation is always its own step, so a switch and a commit are two undos and undo can never roll past a commit by accident. It lost its positional argument and its `--force` and became repeatable — naming one operation is `ff op restore`, which shares the whole mechanism. `ff redo` is the complement, and it reads the pointer's own reflog as a stack, so a second redo reverses the undo before the one the first already took rather than bouncing between two states.

Undo moves a pointer rather than writing an operation, so the log records work and never navigation. What it steps off stays reachable, and new work after an undo forks the log rather than truncating it. The cost, stated rather than discovered later: the log no longer shows that an undo happened.

**One grammar**

`-r` takes a revset. It is gitrevisions entire — every symbol and suffix git accepts, handed through unread — plus the set algebra git has no way to spell: `|` `&` `~` for union, intersection and complement, `..` and `::` for ranges and ancestry, and functions like `on_branch()`, `kind()`, `session()`, `description()` and `base()`.

One grammar spans both address spaces. `ff log -r '::@ & ~(::main)'` asks about commits, `ff op log -r 'session(<id>)'` asks about operations, and the same scanner and parser feed both — the difference between the spaces is what a leaf denotes and which functions exist, never how the text is shaped. `base()` is the single crossing between them: it takes operations and returns the commits they ran on, so `ff log -r 'base(@)'` runs.

Being wrong is never priced by history. Binding resolves every leaf and raises every refusal in O(leaves), so a misspelled branch on a million-commit repository fails in microseconds. Evaluation is lazy and folds set algebra into gix's own walk options rather than materializing around them — `x..y` is literally gix's range and `a & ~(::b)` puts b in the walk's hidden list and allocates nothing — so `-r '::@' -n 25` is twenty-five pops of a frontier at any depth.

Ambiguity is refused rather than ranked. Where a name resolves as both a branch and a commit, fufu names both candidates instead of quietly preferring one and saying nothing about the other; the escapes are `refs/heads/…` for the branch and `commit_id(…)` for the commit. Absences are recognized rather than merely unparseable, because the point is to teach the spelling that works: `x-` names `x^`, `x+` names `x::`, `a ~ b` names `a & ~b`, and `a...b` names `(a..b) | (b..a)`.

One module hands text to gix and a guard test pins it, so what reaches git's parser is always a full ref path, a 40-character sha, or the literal `HEAD`. A differential suite against the real git binary covers every suffix form, abbreviations of every length, reflog and upstream navigation, and the ranges — which makes "gitrevisions entire" a checked claim rather than a wish.

**One contract**

Automation was foreign to fufu by habit rather than by nature: a script, a CI job, or an agent reached for git because fufu offered it nothing better to reach for, and so took git's guarantees instead of fufu's.

Every `--json` output is now `{"ff":1,"cmd":"<verb>","data":{…}}` — one line, terminated once, carrying the contract version and the canonical verb name so a script can assert what it is reading before it parses it.

Errors carry a stable id and the ways out, instead of a sentence that gets reworded next release. The exit code carries the verdict: 0 done or yes, 1 no, 2 the command line was wrong, 3 held — nothing was touched and a human decision is required. The id's namespace carries the class rather than a second field, so `usage/` exits 2 and `held/` exits 3, and it is greppable. `ff explain <id>` prints what one means, the detail, and the exits; `ff explain --list` prints the whole registry. Both work outside a repository and take no snapshot. Fifty-eight ids so far.

A verb computes one model and both renderings read it. `ff status` had assembled its data, handed part to the human renderer, and hand-built JSON from the rest — and the two had already drifted, so reconciled foreign ref motion reached your eyes and never a script's. That class of drift is now structurally impossible rather than merely fixed.

`--json` and `--session` are declared once on the root command and reach every verb, in both positions. `ff --json status` used to be a usage error; the invocation's cross-cutting state is a context built once before dispatch rather than a global read from deep in the call graph.

**The smaller moves**

Naming a branch is `ff describe -b <name>`. `ff branch` had three meanings and the claim was the one that did not belong: saying what a piece of work is, whether the subject is the change's description or the branch's name, is one verb on one axis — `-m` for the change, `-b` for the branch. `ff branch` keeps the bookkeeping, `list` and `delete`, with bare `ff branch` still the list.

`ff restore` splits `--at` into three flags with one kind each: `--from <rev>` through the revset, `--at-op <op>` through the operation log, `--at <time>` through the clock. Bare `ff restore <paths>` now pulls from the commit under the open change rather than from the newest capture, which was nearly a no-op — that gives the everyday "discard my edits to this file" a spelling it did not have.

`ff start <target>` routes through the resolver instead of trying branch names first, so a name that is both a branch and a commit is reported rather than silently forked at one of them. `ff switch <sha>` no longer answers "no branch named ace9a9b": it mints an anonymous branch there and says so.

`ff session` is gone, verb and span model together — a session is a tag on an operation, not a range between two points, and tagged operations need not be contiguous because two agents interleave. The tag survives: `FF_SESSION` and `--session` still stamp it, it rides every row of `ff op log --json`, and `session()` selects on it. Nothing stateful is left behind — the marker file that made `ff session` the only mode in the tool is deleted, so there is nothing to clean up after a crash.

`ff doctor` caught up with the vocabulary: one log row plus identity, branch pointers as pointers, and a reflog row that says why that reflog is load-bearing.

**Speed**

The one rule is that twenty-five rows never charge for the whole log to produce them, and after the merge two views were doing exactly that. `ff op log` had to decode every capture in between to find twenty-five verbs, so operations now state the hop — a written link to the newest non-capture before them, the same trade the segment link already makes. And the id index was reading its unsorted tail one seek-and-read per record, up to five hundred syscalls per id, twelve thousand for a screen of them; it reads the tail whole once and caches it, about 21 KiB.

Against the bench gate's bound of 1.50x per decade of log growth: `ff op log` went 4.41x to 1.12x, `ff evolog` 3.17x to 0.97x, and the four rows already inside the bound moved closer to 1. The whole gate passes.

Correctness in the same area: the operation log takes its own lock. Two racing appends could both succeed with the second silently overwritten — the loser was told it was committed, and then was not on the log. gix's `MustExistAndMatch` reads a ref's value before acquiring its lock, so it guards a stale caller rather than a second writer; fufu now excludes its own writers itself, across the whole span from reading the tip to moving it. A capture never waits, because another is along in a moment; a verb waits two seconds and then reports `ref/contended`, because a verb is something you typed.

**Breaking**

Anything scripting fufu should look before upgrading.

- `--json` output is enveloped. What used to be the whole document is now under `data`, beside `"ff"` and `"cmd"`. Failures emit `{"ff":1,"cmd":…,"error":{…}}` — `error` replacing `data`, never both.
- The reports that carried `pre_snapshot` carry `pre_op` instead, spelled in letters — the thing they point at stopped being a snapshot.
- `ff status --json` gains `foreign` (an array of `ref`/`old`/`new`, or null), and `open.base`, `open.time` and `parent.time`, which the human view had been printing and a script had been handed nothing to derive. No existing key moved.
- `ff log --ops` is retired: `ff op log` is a different command with a different output shape, so it is a removal rather than a rename, and the flag raises a redirect.
- `ff branch <name>` no longer claims a name — `ff describe -b <name>` does. The old spelling raises `usage/unknown-subcommand` and carries the name through to a ready-to-run replacement.
- `ff session` and its `--session` filters on `ff log` and `ff evolog` are gone.
- `ff undo` takes no positional argument and no `--force`. `ff op restore <id>` is the long form.
- `ff restore --at` takes a time and only a time. An operation is `--at-op`, a revision is `--from`; raw hex is never an operation address, and `@{n}` is spelled `--at-op @^`.
- `ff start <unresolvable>` raises `usage/revset-unknown-revision` at exit 2 rather than `target/unresolvable` at exit 1.
- Exit codes are a ladder now, so a failure that used to exit 1 may exit 2 or 3. Bare `ff describe` with no terminal to ask on returns `usage/needs-message` instead of spawning an editor at nobody.

**Upgrading from v0.1.0 or v0.2.0**

The two old logs are not readable by this fufu, and nothing converts them. The first command you run parks every ref that held them under `refs/fufu/legacy/` and tells you it did — copied rather than overwritten, because "fufu never silently destroys history" is worth keeping true even where the history is being abandoned on purpose. Your commits, branches and working tree are untouched; what you lose is the ability to restore from captures taken before the upgrade. If you need one of them, take it before you upgrade.

Install: see the [README](https://github.com/tyler-johnson/fufu#install) — `curl | sh`, PowerShell, or `brew install tyler-johnson/tap/fufu`. Already on v0.2.0? `ff update`.

Binaries for linux/darwin/windows × amd64/arm64, checksummed. The design — what exists, what's coming, and why — lives in [DESIGN.md](https://github.com/tyler-johnson/fufu/blob/main/DESIGN.md).
